chunks: Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix. The question: Why is it important that signals for both lines of the diff pair arrive to the source at the same time?
What happens if they don't arrive at the same time? How can you ensure that they do arrive at the same time?
The receiver of a differential pair expects the two wires to be exact mirror images at the same instant.
If one wire arrives late, for a moment the two wires do not mirror each other, and part of the signal turns into common-mode, which is the same-direction motion on both wires.
That hurts the eye, adds jitter and makes the pair radiate more noise. You fix it by making both traces arrive together.
Picture two rowers in a boat who must pull their oars together. If one is late, the boat does not just slow a little. It also wobbles sideways, because the pulls no longer cancel.
The sideways wobble is the common-mode noise. The forward motion barely changes, which is why the damage is easy to miss.
The common-mode trace (red) should be a flat 1. 2 volts. With a 40 picoseconds skew it develops a pulse of 80 millivolts: V s over 2 change in t over t r equals 0. 2 times 0. 4 .
The differential edge (green) now takes t r plus change in t equals 140 picoseconds instead of 100 picoseconds to complete.
That pulse repeats on every edge and is a clock-rate-related common-mode current.
Skew: the time difference between the two lines of a pair ("Serpentining for bus synchronization"). Common-mode: voltage or current that moves both lines the same way.
It radiates well ("Common-mode voltage of a differential pair"). Mode conversion: signal turning from differential into common-mode because of imbalance.
CMRR: how well a receiver rejects common-mode noise that arrives from outside.
Eye diagram: an overlay of many bits that shows timing and voltage margin ("What an eye diagram shows").
A 3 mm length difference on FR-4 is about 3 times 5. 9 equals 17. 7 picoseconds of skew. The common-mode pulse at each edge peaks near (V s over 2)( change in t over t r) .
For a larger 25 picoseconds skew, with a 0. 4 volts swing and a 100 picoseconds edge, that is 0. 2 times 0. 25 equals 50 millivolts on every edge.
The receiver's CMRR cannot remove it, because the pair made it inside the channel. That is the whole idea.
"If the two lines of a pair don't arrive together, part of the differential signal turns into common-mode.
That's a voltage the receiver ignores, but it's also current that radiates and a signal-dependent disturbance, so skew costs eye width, adds jitter and creates EMI.
The mode conversion, in S-parameter terms, goes as tan of pi times frequency times skew, so 20 picoseconds at 5 gigahertz is about minus 10 decibels.
To avoid it I match the pair in delay, locally at each bend and via, keep everything symmetric, and verify with TDR or an eye diagram."
